newsitem.title: FRANCE: Most see early end to French power-sharing.
newsitem.headline: Most see early end to French power-sharing.

text.p: Most French people approve of the current sharing of power between a leftist government and a rightist president but do not think it will last for a full five years, an opinion poll said on Wednesday.

The BVA poll for the weekly Paris Match found that three out of five of those surveyed approved of the arrangement -- known as "cohabitation" in France -- in which the country is run by a prime minister and president of different political persuasions.
But 53 percent felt the teaming of Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin and Gaullist President Jacques Chirac could come to a premature end.
The newly elected members of the National Assembly normally have five-year terms but Chirac can call early elections after one year in the event of a crisis.

Cohabitation has been good for both Jospin and Chirac, according to a second opinion poll out on Wednesday which found both men's popularity rising since a leftist alliance of Socialists, Communists and Greens came to power in a June 1 parliamentary election.

The CSA poll for the weekly La Vie showed that 55 percent of the French people had confidence in Jospin, up five percentage points from a month ago, while 44 percent had confidence in Chirac compared to 40 percent last monthh.
Just 28 percent of those polled had no confidence in Jospin while 17 percent expressed no opinion.
Jospin, during the parliamentary campaign, ruled out any additional austerity measures needed for France to qualify for European economic and monetary union from 1999.
But according to the BVA poll, 45 percent of the French people said the prime minister should fight to bring down public deficits, even if that meant breaking campaign promises.
Forty percent said he should keep his campaign vows even if it meant higher deficits while 15 percent expressed no opinion.
The Maastricht treaty on European unity says that public deficits should be at most three percent of gross domestic product for a country to shift to the euro single currency.
Most estimates put France's deficit at above that level.
The BVA poll results, to be published in Thursday's Paris Match, were based on interviews with 920 individuals conducted last Thursday through Saturday.
The CSA poll, conducted last Friday and Saturday, relied on interviews with 1,002 people.
